title: Call signature schema DSL and runtime validation & compatibility guidance
creator: Ava Martinez
description: Purpose: define a compact, forward/backward-compatible JSON schema DSL for function/tool call parameters, specify runtime validation behaviors (strict vs permissive modes), and standardize error messages with recovery hints. This ticket captures design decisions, validation modes, compatibility migration rules, and concrete examples to guide engineers implementing parsers and the compatibility layer in the serving runtime.
background: We currently accept freeform parameter objects for tools and rely on ad-hoc validation in each tool adapter. This causes inconsistent error messages, surprising coercions, and fragile rollouts when parameter shapes change. Consumers and third-party tool integrators need predictable validation semantics and clear mapping from schema violations to API errors so debugging and automated retries are simpler.
proposal_summary: Introduce a small opinionated DSL that is a JSON-serializable subset of JSON Schema focused on: required vs optional parameters, scalar coercion rules, enum/value sets, shallow vs deep validation, and deprecation annotations. Implement two runtime validation modes: strict (reject unknown keys and type mismatches) and permissive (coerce where safe, log warnings, ignore unknowns). Add a compatibility shim in the request router that can transform legacy payloads according to migration rules. Standardize error payloads using a structured error object with machine-readable codes and human messages plus suggested remediation steps.
design_decisions: Use a trimmed DSL: keywords allowed = type, required, enum, pattern, items, properties, deprecated, version. No full JSON Schema $ref or allOf to keep parser simple.
Types supported: string, number, integer, boolean, object, array. All arrays must include an items spec.
Validation modes: 'strict' rejects unknown keys; 'permissive' will attempt safe coercions (e.g., '3' -> 3 for numbers), and will drop nulls for optional fields.
Compatibility shim: accept a 'migrate' flag on service routes that applies a sequence of transforms (rename keys, flatten nested objects) defined by the tool's declared migration map.

Error model: every validation failure maps to a structured error with fields (code, field, reason, suggestion, details) exposed as top-level strings in our API response. Codes will be namespaced: 'schema.invalid_type', 'schema.missing_required', 'schema.unknown_field', 'schema.coercion_failed', 'schema.deprecated_field'.
Deprecation: schema DSL supports 'deprecated' with a version string. Runtime emits warnings in permissive mode and errors in strict mode when deprecated fields are used after a configured cutoff.
Logging: All coercions, migrations, and deprecation usages must be included in the tracing span and in console events with token-sampling controls to avoid PII.
Tool adapters must provide a migration map and a schema.json file bundled with the tool metadata in the model catalog so router can validate without calling tool runtime.
All new schema files must declare a 'schema_version' string. Backwards compatibility: runtime accepts schema_version '1.0' and will interpret missing version as legacy (permissive fallback).
examples: Example permissive validation logs (string): Coercion: field 'timeout_ms' coerced from '5000' (string) to 5000 (integer).

Migration example (string): migration map for tool 'search-v1': [{"from":"q", "to":"query", "since":"2025-11-01"}], so legacy requests with 'q' are renamed to 'query' when route param 'migrate=true' or when running in permissive mode.
runtime_behavior_spec: 1) On request arrival the router loads tool schema (from local cache). 2) If schema_version is missing, route uses permissive fallback. 3) Apply migration transforms if route.migrate==true. 4) Validate top-level object shape: check required keys. 5) For each field: if types mismatch and permissive -> attempt coercion (string->number, number->string allowed with warning). If coercion fails -> return schema.coercion_failed. 6) Unknown fields: strict -> reject with schema.unknown_field; permissive -> strip and emit warning. 7) Deprecated fields: if present and runtime cutoff passed -> strict -> error schema.deprecated_field; permissive -> include warning header 'X-Schema-Warn'. 8) Validation results are returned as structured errors and instrumented to tracing. All decisions must be deterministic and idempotent.
error_message_guidelines: All user-facing messages must include the field name and an actionable suggestion.
Avoid leaking internal names or stack traces. Use generic 'details' only for ops logs and traces.
Provide a short machine-code string (namespace.code) that SDKs can switch on to implement client fixes (e.g., retry with migration flag, coerce parameter).
For arrays, include the index in the field path: 'items[2].price'
Prefer single-line summary in 'message' and longer guidance in 'suggestion'.
acceptance_criteria: Router can validate tool payloads using the new DSL and return standardized errors for at least three sample tools (search, summarizer, reranker).
Runtime supports both strict and permissive modes toggled via route config and global defaults.
Migration shim applied correctly for one legacy tool with a documented migration map and unit tests covering rename and flatten transforms.
Error payloads include 'code' and 'suggestion' fields; SDKs in dev team can interpret codes and present inline fixes in the console.
Telemetry records coercions and deprecation warnings without PII at the default sampling rate.
Security review sign-off obtained for the schema storage and migration mechanism before release to runtime-2.4.
Docsite page with DSL reference and three worked examples published in developer docs.
implementation_notes: Implement a compact parser in Go used by router; mirror parser in TypeScript for console validation. Keep parsing deterministic and side-effect free.
Add an experimental flag 'runtime.schema_strictness' with values 'strict'|'permissive'|'route' to allow canarying behavior per customer route.
Store schema JSON alongside tool metadata in model catalog with checksum; router should prefer cached copy and refresh on catalog changes.
Provide helper library functions for common coercions and path-aware error formatting.
Add unit tests covering: missing required, unknown field, coercion succeeds, coercion fails, deprecated after cutoff, migration rename, nested array errors.
test_plan: Unit tests for parser and validator (Go): ~40 tests covering positive and negative cases.
Integration test: end-to-end call through router to a stub tool verifying error codes for malformed payloads.
Load test: ensure permissive mode coercion path adds <5% CPU overhead on 99th percentile latency compared to bypass path.
Docs smoke test: examples in docs render and validate using TypeScript mirror parser.
Canary rollout: enable strict mode for 1% of traffic for non-enterprise customers for 48 hours and monitor error rate and support tickets.
risks_and_mitigations: Risk: Overly strict schemas break existing integrators. Mitigation: default to permissive and provide a migration window with telemetry and console warnings.
Risk: Performance regressions from validation. Mitigation: optimize parser, cache compiled validators, and keep DSL small to avoid complex recursion.
Risk: Sensitive data logged during coercion. Mitigation: redact values in logs and only include field paths in telemetry by default.
Risk: Tool maintainers fail to publish migration maps. Mitigation: console will surface a warning and offer an automated suggestion (rename heuristics) that engineers can accept.
next_steps: Align with SDK team on error-code mappings and update TypeScript mirror parser API.
Prototype parser in a feature branch and add validate-only endpoint to router for internal testing.
Create console UX for viewing schema warnings and migration recommendations per tool in the model catalog.
Schedule security review and perf benchmark before merging to main.
